name: Lena Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, AI firms, unions and government. Your answers are confidential. What do you do on a normal workday?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 43 and came back into office work with a bachelor’s degree in accounting, but I am still a junior here. I sort invoices, prepare the first draft of accounts and tax returns, and use the approved AI tool every day to flag odd bills. I like tracking an error to the actual receipt, though the senior reviewer still catches things I miss. Reopening a file just before leaving to collect the children wears me out.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does the week look like at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Jules, my partner, loads orders at a warehouse, and our two children are in school. The mortgage and our low pay leave less than a month of expenses saved, so I teach two neighbours’ children maths on Saturdays for extra money. There are few other accounting jobs nearby, and I am quick to try a tool if it helps me learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team the small shortcuts can give us a few minutes to call clients about unclear bills. I still want the purchase invoices checked before any return goes out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our budget is already narrow because my junior wage is low and the mortgage is fixed every month. I have less than one month saved; a small software gain helps the queue but does not protect us from a missed shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep using the approved AI tool I use each day to sort invoice questions, then check its output against source papers. In the first year I would keep the same tax files and put the 15 a week I earn from Saturday maths tutoring into a separate mortgage account, if those lessons continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about household money even with an easy AI picture. The approved invoice tool is familiar; the bank balance is the hard part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are you tutoring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two neighbours’ children come to our dining table on Saturdays for maths, and their parents pay me after each lesson. I began last winter when the washing machine broke.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What mistake did the approved tool make?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It put a plumber’s home repair bill into a client’s business costs. I flagged the address and asked our senior reviewer to check it before we corrected the draft.

say: I would use small **time savings** to ask clients about unclear bills.
I would still check **purchase invoices** before filing tax returns.
think: Our **mortgage** and my low junior pay already make the budget narrow.
Less than one month saved leaves us exposed to a **missed shift**.
do: Keep using my **daily approved tool** and check invoice flags against source papers.
Put **Saturday tutoring pay** into a separate mortgage account while lessons continue.
feel: I feel **anxious** about household money despite stable work.
S0.quote: The approved invoice tool is familiar; the bank balance is the hard part.
fieldNote: Her **daily AI use** is already routine and checked against original papers; the repair-bill error shows she does not trust output blindly.
The **tutoring income** is an existing side stream for the mortgage, conditional on the neighbours continuing lessons.

steps.text: Keep sorting client invoices with approved tool and checking source papers
Put Saturday tutoring pay into mortgage account while lessons continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the firm to let juniors learn to check AI drafts instead of quietly cutting their shifts. A wrong expense still lands on the client’s tax bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do the routine account and tax first passes, so I expect the software to take most of my weekly junior hours. The mortgage depends on my pay and my partner’s warehouse shifts; under one month saved will not carry us far.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the senior reviewer for paid time to test the approved draft checker on four client files and write down each correction. I would add one extra Saturday maths lesson if a neighbour wants it; in the first year, if the firm cuts my hours, I would apply for a vacant accounts-payable post at the warehouse where my partner works, but only with written pay and hours at least equal to this job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about losing hours, even though I like learning the new tools. I cannot tell the lender that I was curious and hope they wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the warehouse first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my partner Jules to tell me when an accounts-payable post is actually advertised, then apply through the normal process. I would not assume a family connection means an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would an extra lesson bring?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Another 15 a week if a parent books it, not a guaranteed wage. I would keep that separate from the mortgage payment until the booking is regular.

say: I would ask the firm to **teach juniors** to check AI drafts.
I would remind colleagues a **wrong expense** still reaches a client’s tax bill.
think: I expect software to remove most of my **junior hours**.
Our **mortgage** cannot wait on a savings cushion under one month.
do: Test the **approved draft checker** on four files only if the senior reviewer grants paid time.
Offer one **extra maths lesson** only if a parent books it.
Apply for an **advertised warehouse accounts post** after cuts, with written pay and hours at least equal to now.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about lost hours despite liking the tools.
S1.quote: I cannot tell the lender that I was curious and hope they wait.
fieldNote: She is **fast with tools**, but sees that learning alone cannot meet a mortgage payment if junior hours fall.
Her **warehouse fallback** depends on an advertised vacancy and written equivalent pay and hours; family contact is only a source of information.

steps.text: Test approved checker on four files only if senior reviewer grants paid time
Offer extra Saturday maths lesson only if parent books
Apply for advertised warehouse accounts post after cuts with written equal pay and hours

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2028 can do our accounts and tax thinking work in 2028, before the capable robots around 2031. I would ask the firm to tell juniors the truth about shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect most of my junior checking hours to go once AGI can do the thinking cheaper. My daily AI practice may help me spot errors, but it will not replace our low wage if the firm cuts the roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask for a written hours forecast and contact both tutoring families about a regular Saturday schedule, without counting their replies as income yet. If my hours fall in the first year after 2028, I would apply for an advertised warehouse accounts job with written pay and hours at least equal to mine; if no vacancy is open, I would ask my partner Jules to cover the next mortgage payment from confirmed extra warehouse shifts while I search nearby firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because there is less than a month between us and a missed mortgage payment. A written hours forecast does not put mortgage money in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could Jules take those shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jules loads orders at the warehouse, and overtime appears some weeks but not others. We would budget it only after the shift is confirmed and paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our two school-age children we are keeping weekends cheap for a while. I do not want them carrying the mortgage worry into class.

say: I would say **AGI by 2028** reaches account screens before capable robots arrive.
I would ask for an **honest shift forecast** for junior staff.
think: I expect most **junior checking hours** to go after 2028.
Daily AI use will not replace my **low wage** if shifts disappear.
do: Seek a **written roster forecast** and ask tutoring families about regular Saturdays.
After cuts, apply for an **advertised warehouse vacancy** with written equal pay and hours.
If no vacancy opens, ask **partner Jules** for mortgage help only from confirmed, paid extra warehouse shifts.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because one missed payment is close.
S2.quote: A written hours forecast does not put mortgage money in the account.
fieldNote: Her **daily tool practice** gives confidence with drafts but no protection from a lost junior wage in 2028.
She counts **tutoring and overtime** only when confirmed; a warehouse move needs an advertised vacancy and written terms.

steps.text: Ask existing tutoring families about regular Saturdays without budgeting unconfirmed pay
Apply for advertised warehouse vacancy with written equal pay and hours or search nearby firms
Ask partner Jules for mortgage help from confirmed, paid shifts after cuts if no vacancy opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my team AGI by 2031 gives us time to learn which client checks still need people. The capable robots around 2034 are later than the change to our tax screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me build a proper mortgage buffer and gain work with clients, but the first-pass tax tasks can still disappear. I would not treat my AI skill as a promise of a full week’s pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the manager for a paid client-query shift each fortnight, if the senior reviewer agrees I can handle the calls. I would save 50 a month from tutoring while lessons and both wages hold; in the first year after 2031 I would take a vacant paid client-service post only with written salary and hours at least equal to my current job, or keep remaining tax hours while applying to advertised nearby posts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though I have time to earn the trust of clients. The plan still needs a vacancy and steady wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you practise on the query shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would explain missing receipts to small shop owners, then ask the senior reviewer to check the advice I gave. I still need practice with awkward calls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the manager says no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the manager refuses a paid shift, I would keep the tax files I have and ask for a reason I can work on. I would not leave a paying junior post for an unpaid promise of client work.

say: I would use the **five-year runway** to learn client checks.
I would tell colleagues the **tax screens** change before robots arrive.
think: My **first-pass tasks** could disappear even if I gain client skills.
AI fluency does not guarantee a **full week’s pay**.
do: Seek an approved **paid client-query shift** fortnightly; if refused, keep current tax files.
Save **50 monthly** from tutoring while lessons and both wages hold.
Take a **client-service vacancy** after 2031 with written equal salary and hours, or seek posted jobs while employed.
feel: I feel **anxious** because the plan needs steady wages and an opening.
S3.quote: I would not leave a paying junior post for an unpaid promise of client work.
fieldNote: She wants **supervised client calls** and a paid shift, which recognizes that her current junior skill needs practice.
Her **savings** depend on tutoring and both wages; later client work needs a vacancy with written equivalent pay and hours.

steps.text: Learn client queries in paid fortnightly shift if manager and senior reviewer approve
Save 50 monthly from tutoring while lessons and both wages hold
Take client-service vacancy with written equal pay and hours after 2031 or seek vacancies while employed
Keep current tax files if paid client-query shift is refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say AGI by 2036 gives families time to prepare, but the accounts desk changes in 2036, not when robots arrive around 2039. I would want the firm to publish its training plan early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years could let us lower the mortgage and build savings while the children move through school. I still expect my routine checks to go when AGI arrives, but I could have a stronger client role by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would keep doing tax files and ask the partner to let me shadow our senior reviewer on harder AI checks, then train one new junior each quarter, with paid time if approved. I would put 75 a month toward the mortgage principal after we first build two monthly payments in cash, while both wages hold; in the first year after 2036 I would stay in a paid client-support post only with written salary and hours at least equal to now, or apply for an advertised local post before leaving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about 2036 but more settled about the next few years. A decade lets us protect the children’s home while I prove what I can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach the new junior?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show the original invoice beside the AI draft and ask them to explain any mismatch to me. I would not mark a file correct just because software made it quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why build cash before paying down the loan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lower mortgage balance cannot pay the plumber tomorrow if the boiler fails. Two mortgage payments in cash would let us handle a short interruption without borrowing.

say: I would ask for an **early training plan** before 2036.
I would remind colleagues the **accounts desk** changes before hands-on robots arrive.
think: I expect routine **checking tasks** to go after 2036.
Ten years could build a **mortgage reserve** and paid client skills.
do: Keep **tax files** and learn harder AI checks from our senior reviewer before teaching juniors, with partner approval and paid time.
Build **two cash payments**, then pay 75 monthly against principal while both wages hold.
Keep **client-support work** after 2036 with written equal salary and hours; otherwise seek advertised local work before leaving.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about 2036 but steadier over the next few years.
S4.quote: A lower mortgage balance cannot pay the plumber tomorrow if the boiler fails.
fieldNote: Her **cash-before-principal** sequence protects the family from ordinary repairs before making extra mortgage payments.
She wants **paid teaching time** and partner approval, while the later client-support role requires written equivalent pay and hours.

steps.text: Keep doing current tax files while paid hours remain
Shadow senior AI reviews then train junior quarterly if partner approves paid time
Build two cash payments then pay 75 monthly against mortgage while both wages hold
Keep client-support post with written equal pay and hours after 2036 or seek vacancies before leaving

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because routine account work could leave the junior roster before we have one mortgage payment saved. A written hours forecast, paid client training and a real vacancy would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether using AI daily makes me feel secure. Knowing which button found an error does not mean the firm still needs my whole shift.

headlineQuote: Knowing which button found an error does not mean the firm still needs my whole shift.
portrait: At **43**, Lena is a junior accountant with a bachelor’s degree, still learning tax and accounts work while using AI daily.
She and **partner Jules** have two school-age children, a mortgage, low pay and less than one month saved.
She earns **Saturday tutoring money** and has few local accounting options, but readily tests new tools and supervised client work.
The **2028 scenario** threatens her junior hours; longer runways support a conditional cash reserve and paid client role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove her routine junior hours before the household saves one mortgage payment.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **written forecast**, paid client training and an actual vacancy.
